p.title: How Dark Is It? An Investigation of Dark Money Operations in U.S. Nonprofit Political Advocacy Organizations

ext.title: How Dark Is It? An Investigation of Dark Money Operations in U.S. Nonprofit Political Advocacy Organizations
ext.venue: Nonprofit Policy Forum 14(2): 101-129 (received July 15, 2022; accepted February 28, 2023)
ext.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; empirical index construction and validation (open access, CC BY 4.0)
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text in two chunks (lines 1-1591 and 1592-2172 of 2172), covering abstract, introduction, theory, context, sample, index construction (all nine components), correlation tables, results, OpenSecrets validation, discussion, conclusion and references. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this PDF (task specified "(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Extracted tables 2-4 are garbled in the text layer (cell values largely missing), so table-level numbers are not reconstructed beyond what the prose states.
ext.research_question: Can observable characteristics in IRS Form 990 filings and one website measure be combined into a transparency (versus opaqueness) index that ranks social welfare 501(c)(4) economic policy advocacy organizations on how likely they are to be vehicles for dark money political activity? Secondary: under what conditions would a high net worth donor benefit from keeping advocacy operations low-profile (p.105-106)?
ext.theory: Combined theory. (1) Elite theory (Gen and Wright 2018): political power is held by a small upper-class segment with uniform preferences that intentionally perpetuates its privileges. (2) Weisbrod (1991) heterogeneous-preferences model: a median voter sets the level of tax-funded service provision; donors with preferences far from the median can fund advocacy to move the median voter. Combined, elites may move the median voter away from the median position and have reasons to stay invisible: insider tactics can yield only temporary wins if voters later punish lawmakers (p.104-105); unpopular causes need broad support, so a funder's identity is a liability (astroturf and authenticity, Walker 2014; "big bad opponent," Gen and Wright 2018; local-donor trust in high-stakes races; avoiding association with negative messaging) (p.105-106).
ext.data: Unit: organization (social welfare 501(c)(4) advocacy organizations active in U.S. or state-level economic policy). N = 54 organizations: 25 right-leaning, 2 centrist, 27 left-leaning (p.110). Sources: IRS Form 990 (Part I lines 4, 6, 9, 15, 16b, 18; Part IX line 11d; Part X line 27; Schedule C Part I-A line 1; Schedule R), website word counts (Weglot counter; seven sites hand-counted), Form 990 expense data for 2015 and 2016, and the OpenSecrets 2016 dark-money list (95 organizations nationally; 13 of the 54 sample organizations appear). Period: fiscal data for 2016 (presidential election year), with 2015 comparison for expense growth; economic policy verbiage checked for 2017; the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (December 2017) context. Sample rules: founded 2015 or earlier; 2016 total revenue above $100,000; at least four economic policy items on website (testimony, podcasts, blogs, research reports, convenings, press releases) in 2017; sourced from think-tank lists, partisan networks, Post and Boris (2020), and donor-advised fund grantee lists. Author states the dataset covers the population of active organizations in this arena in 2016 (p.110-111). U.S. data only.
ext.method: Descriptive and correlational index construction. Nine components each scaled to 0-1 and summed (maximum 9.0, unweighted by design). Pearson bivariate correlation matrix among components (Table 2, two-tailed significance). Validation against an external watchdog label: second Pearson matrix of the OpenSecrets binary designation against the nine components, plus a logistic regression of OpenSecrets designation on the total index with controls for political lean, natural log of total expenses and founding year; Nagelkerke R-squared reported (p.124). Qualitative case discussion of high-index organizations (p.124-125).
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. Validity is assessed by convergent correlation of components with the OpenSecrets dark-money label and a logistic regression with controls. The author notes the sample was chosen by advocacy topic, not by transparency, so the logistic result (index not significant) is interpreted as a sample-design limitation, and validity is argued from component correlations instead (p.124).
ext.scope: Population: 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations active in U.S. (and state-level) economic policy advocacy, 2016 filings. Institution: U.S. tax-exempt advocacy sector and its links to 501(c)(3) think tanks, 527 organizations and Super PACs. Era: 2015-2017 data, published 2023. The author argues the index transfers to other issue areas (education, Social Security, energy, judicial reform, voting restrictions) but this is not tested (p.109, 125).

key_findings.finding: Index values range from 0.8 (Fix the Debt Coalition Inc.) to 8.3 (Majority Forward), out of a possible 9.0.

Index bands: up to 3.0 transparent; 3.0-5.0 some opaque characteristics (contentious band; includes Americans for Prosperity and Open Society Policy Center); 5.0-7.0 quite opaque; above 7.0 very opaque, including many large advocacy groups with very small boards, sparse websites and no staff.
Anomaly cases: One Nation spent $63.3M in 2016 (up from $7.1M in 2015), had one board member, and gave $21.7M to the Senate Leadership Fund (PAC at the same address).
Majority Forward spent $35.8M in 2016 with salaries at 1.34% of expenses, an 81-word website and two board members.

Freedom Frontier spent $5.9M in 2016 (up from $873,707 in 2015); $6.2M of revenue came entirely from grants and contributions with no fundraising expense; almost 75% of expenses went to political activity, including a $4.4M grant to a PAC.
Organizations rely heavily on donated revenue, averaging 92% of total revenue; the data cannot show whether that comes from few large donors or many small donors.
key_findings.numbers: mean 92% of revenue from grants and contributions

key_findings.finding: Almost all index components are positively correlated with each other; the single negative correlation is not significant. Salaries as a percent of expenses is the component most strongly correlated with the others.
Only two organizations had membership revenue (Maine People's Alliance; Utah Taxpayers Association), so membership was dropped from the index.
Three mid-sized organizations had boards of 26, 34 and 37 members, truncated to 25 for the board component.
Two organizations had fundraising expenses exceeding grants and contributions; that component was truncated at zero.

Validation: 13 of the 54 sample organizations appear on the OpenSecrets 2016 dark-money list of 95 national groups. The OpenSecrets binary label is significantly correlated with four components: related to a 527, political spending as a percent of expenses, salaries as a percent of expenses, and unrestricted net assets as a percent of expenses.
key_findings.numbers: 13 of 54; OpenSecrets list 95 orgs; 4 significant component correlations

key_findings.finding: Logistic regression of OpenSecrets designation on the total index (controls: lean, ln total expenses, founding year) is not significant for the index. Only total expenses is significant (larger organizations more likely listed). Political lean is not significant. Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.529.
key_findings.numbers: Nagelkerke R2 = 0.529; only ln total expenses significant

key_findings.finding: Political spending across this sample is described as strongly negative, asking voters to defeat candidates, per FEC filings reported by Beckel (2018).
key_findings.numbers: qualitative; no count given in text

key_findings.finding: Expenses rose sharply between 2015 and 2016 (a presidential year). The author considered an expense-growth component and excluded it because political spending peaks in presidential years for any organization.

Context: in the year before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (December 2017), polls showed broad majority support for raising taxes on the wealthy (Gallup 2017; Pew 2017; Reuters/Ipsos 2017), and the author treats the 2016 set as a window onto a conservative tax-policy win.

Author concludes high-index C4s look like elite issue entrepreneurs (Goss 2016) under a strict sense: a single donor or few donors may control the C4 as a for-profit firm. Author argues this challenges the C4 definition of promoting general welfare and that C4 use as a conduit around FEC individual limits resembles straw donation; recommends publicly reporting the largest donors behind C4 political funding.

measures: Index (0-9, sum of nine components, unweighted): transparency/opacity composite. Higher = more opaque.
C1 Board size (Form 990 Part I line 4): 1 - min(board size, 25)/25; takes greater of C4 and related 501(c)(3) board.
C2 Volunteers (Part I line 6): 0 if reported 0 or blank, 1 if volunteers used; recorded as one minus value so the scale matches transparency direction.
C3 Website words: 1 - min(word count, 100,000)/100,000; related 501(c)(3) or 527 site used as proxy when C4 has none.
C4 Related to a 527 (Schedule R): 0 if none, 1 if one or more related 527s; scaled to 0-1 in the index.
C5 Related to a 501(c)(3) (Schedule R): 0 if related to one or more 501(c)(3)s, 1 if not.
C6 Grants to political organizations or lobbying scaled by total expenses (Schedule C Part I-A line 1 plus Part IX line 11d); text does not print the exact 0-1 transform for this component.
C7 Salaries: 1 - total salaries (Part I line 15) / total expenses (Part I line 18). Consultant fees excluded unless employee-based; contractor data not split.
C8 Unrestricted net assets (Part X line 27): 1 - UNA / (3 x total expenses), negative UNA set to zero; three years of expenses treated as generous savings target.
C9 Fundraising: 1 - fundraising expenses (Part I line 16b) / grants and contributions (Part I line 9), truncated at zero.
Political-intensity measure (expense increase in presidential vs non-presidential year) and membership revenue were considered and excluded.
limitations: No perfect external validation source exists because the process is anonymous; the OpenSecrets list is acknowledged as flawed.
Every component measures legal behavior; concern arises only from combinations, and the author accepts this rests on judgment.

Index construction involves truncation of outliers (board size at 25, website words at 100,000, UNA at 3x expenses, fundraising at zero) that are value judgments; OECD (2008) is cited on weighting and truncation.
Equal weighting is a deliberate simplicity choice, but the author notes organizations would argue for different weights that favor them.
Form 990 data become public only after two or more years, so organizations can operate unscrutinized for a period.
Small N (54) limits statistical power; the logistic regression Nagelkerke R2 of 0.529 is described as reflecting the small dataset; index was not significant against OpenSecrets labels.
Sample was selected on advocacy topic, not on transparency, so the index's validation depends on correlations rather than the OpenSecrets test.
Grants between C4s are not classified as political or issue spending, so some political flows are excluded from C6.
Website word counts are hand-counted for seven sites and use related-organization proxies for some C4s.
Expense and program data are from one presidential year (2016), so cycle-level variation is not modeled.
Fiscal-year and 2017 website verbiage are used for inclusion, so cross-year timing differences are not fully aligned.
Index is applicable only to the U.S. context; generalization to other issue areas is argued but not tested.
Several tables (2-4) are only partially recoverable from the extracted text layer; table-level values could not be fully verified from the text.
references_of_note: Gen and Wright 2018 (Policy Studies Journal 46(2): 298-326): Q-methodology on advocacy strategies; source of elite-theory tenets and the 'big bad opponent' quote used in the theory section.
Weisbrod 1991 (The Nonprofit Economy): heterogeneous-preferences model underlying the combined median-voter theory.
Mayer 2016 (Dark Money) and Mayer 2018 (Journal of Legislation 45(2): 194-234): dark-money mechanics and 501(c)(4) soft-law regulation.
Page, Seawright and Lacombe 2018 (Billionaires and Stealth Politics): stealth political activity by billionaires; cited for stealth tactics.
Goss 2016 (Politics Symposium 49(3): 442-8): 'policy plutocrats' and elite issue entrepreneurs.
Skocpol 2020: elites advocating for elite preferences.
Plehwe, Neujeffski and Kramer 2018 (Policy and Society 37(2): 188-205): highly networked austerity think-tank networks in the EU; relevant to advocacy networks.
Irvin and Sokolowski 2020 (Nonprofit Policy Forum 11(1)): counts 190+ tax-policy think tanks and advocacy organizations in the U.S.; sample-frame antecedent.
Walker 2014 (Grassroots for Hire) and Walker 1991 (Mobilizing Interest Groups): astroturf and insider/outsider advocacy.
Nelson 2019 (Shadow Network): radical-right media and money network; cited for app-based canvassing and shadow networks.
Mosley 2011 (Social Science Review 84(1)): organizational resources and policy advocacy involvement.
Prentice and Brudney 2017 (Voluntas 28(3)): insider and outsider lobbying strategy.
Galle 2020 (American Law and Economics Review 22(2)): tax policy and donations to 501(c)(4)s as a dark-money subsidy.
Choma 2012 (OpenSecrets) and Beckel 2018 (IssueOne): network and negative-spending evidence for 501(c)(4) money flows.
Irvin and Furneaux 2021 (Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly): reserves and unrestricted net assets, used for the UNA component.
Pautz 2014 (Politics 34(4)): UK think-tank collaborative and communicative networks.

rel.summary_md:
Irvin builds a nine-part opacity index from IRS Form 990 fields, plus one website word count, and applies it to 54 501(c)(4) economic-policy advocacy groups using 2016 filings (25 right-leaning, 2 centrist, 27 left-leaning). The components are board size, volunteers, website length, related 527s, related 501(c)(3)s, the share of spending that is political or lobbying, the salary share, the size of reserves and fundraising intensity. Each is scaled 0-1 and the nine are summed with equal weight, so the index runs 0-9. Scores ranged from 0.8 to 8.3. The most opaque groups had one or two board members, almost no staff, very short websites and large grants to affiliated PACs. For example, One Nation spent $63.3M in 2016 and granted $21.7M to the Senate Leadership Fund. Validation is weak. Thirteen of the 54 groups appear on OpenSecrets' 2016 dark-money list, and that label correlates with four of the nine components. But in a logistic regression with controls, the total index does not predict the label (Nagelkerke R2 0.529; only log expenses is significant). The paper also describes this political spending as mostly negative, based on Beckel 2018, without a count.

For Paul's systems this matters mainly in Mentat. The transfer graph traces only FEC committee-to-committee transfers (24G/24K). Money a 501(c)(4) gives a Super PAC therefore enters as a receipt with no upstream path. Separately, under Paul's 2026-07-18 ruling, 501c recipients are excluded from reported totals. The paper shows that excluded group mixes transparent policy shops with near-shell political vehicles. It does not show that the index can tell them apart reliably. Nothing in the paper bears on Melange's member ranking, stance, SNA or Terrier.

bearings.paper_claim: High-opacity C4s send money into FEC committees as grants rather than committee transfers. One Nation granted $21.7M to the Senate Leadership Fund (a PAC at the same address) out of $63.3M spent in 2016. Freedom Frontier gave a $4.4M grant to a PAC, with about 75% of its expenses political. Grants from one C4 to another are not even classed as political on the 990, so those flows drop out of the paper's own index (C6).
bearings.system_side: The graph is built from OTH 24G/24K committee-to-committee records only, with nodes matched by the C######## committee-ID pattern. A non-committee donor such as a 501(c)(4) has no node. Its contribution to a Super PAC appears only as a receipt into that committee, so allocate() cannot trace funding back past the Super PAC. The 'support/oppose/party' buckets therefore attribute Super PAC money by where it goes, never to who funded it upstream.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over for federal Super PAC and Carey-PAC flows from 2010 on, where C4s are disclosed only as contributors. The paper's sample is economic-policy C4s in the 2016 cycle; Mentat covers 2022-2026 industry PACs. How much C4 money reaches industry-linked Super PACs (e.g. crypto's Fairshake) is not measured here. This is a structural blind spot, not a size estimate.

bearings.paper_claim: Political spending by this C4 sample is described as strongly negative, asking voters to defeat candidates (citing FEC filings via Beckel 2018). The paper gives no count or share.
bearings.system_side: Beneficiary attribution keeps opposition money on the named target ('Opposition stays with the named target, never its rivals'). According to the component description (not re-verified here), 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak directional agreement only. The paper's claim is qualitative and second-hand, about C4-linked spending in 2016. Mentat's 89% is for industry Super PAC beneficiary dollars in a different window and denominator. Do not present this as confirming the 89% figure.

bearings.paper_claim: 501(c)(4)s differ widely: opacity scores run from 0.8 to 8.3 on a 0-9 scale. Groups scoring above 7 look like political conduits (tiny boards, no staff, large PAC grants), while those below 3 look like transparent policy organizations. Donations make up a mean 92% of revenue. But the total index did not predict OpenSecrets' dark-money label once controls were added (N=54; only ln expenses was significant).
bearings.paper_location: Section 10 p.118-119; Section 9.9 p.116-117; Section 11 p.123-124
bearings.system_side: Per Paul's ruling of 2026-07-18 (527s and 501c's EXCLUDED), recipients hand-marked 501c in the category workbook are kept as classified rows but tagged EXCLUDED_527_501C and dropped from reported totals as one block. No distinction is made between transparent and conduit-like C4s.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Changing the exclusion is Paul's decision under an owner ruling; this bearing is not a recommendation to change it. Splitting the bucket would need Form 990 data, which Mentat does not collect and which is published two or more years late. The index is also unvalidated (null logistic result, one year, 54 economic-policy groups). At most it could be a display-only flag labeled as a heuristic. Every 501c row is kept, so a split would be possible without re-collecting.

gaps_exposed: Mentat has no nodes for non-committee entities. A 501(c)(4) or IRS-only 527 that funds a Super PAC appears as an untraceable receipt, so upstream industry money routed through C4s is invisible to allocate() (fec_transfer_graph.py:1-6, 484-571).

Mentat does not use IRS Form 990, Schedule R or Schedule C. Related-organization links (C4 to 501(c)(3) to 527 to PAC at a shared address, as with One Nation and the Senate Leadership Fund) cannot be represented.
The block exclusion of 501c recipients (report.R:3175-3177) cannot tell a policy C4 from a conduit-like C4. There is no recipient-level transparency attribute, even as display-only.
Mentat totals are not checked against an external dark-money list such as OpenSecrets' C4 list, so there is no estimate of how much industry money moves through excluded 501c recipients.
flags: The index is unvalidated. Against OpenSecrets labels, the total index is not significant (N=54, 2016 filings, Nagelkerke R2 0.529, only ln expenses significant). Any use in Mentat must carry an UNVALIDATED heuristic label, with its window (2016 filings) and denominator (54 economic-policy C4s). It must never be presented as a probability that an organization is dark money.

The weights are equal and the cut-offs (25 board seats, 100,000 words, three years of expenses) are the author's judgment, much like the uncalibrated constants elsewhere in the system. Treat them as owner-judgment-grade, not estimates.

Mentat's 501c exclusion is Paul's ruling of 2026-07-18. The paper is grounds for raising a question with Paul, not for an agent to change the exclusion. Money collection is frozen per Paul's standing directive.
The paper's elite-theory framing (elites moving the median voter) is a theory, not an identified effect. Do not carry its influence language onto Mentat flow edges.
Any agent estimate of the C4 money flowing into Mentat-tracked Super PACs stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Tables 2-4 were garbled in the extracted text, so correlation magnitudes are not available.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations of this paper; it appears only as an on-disk citation for transfer-graph-and-direction. His recorded view links dark-money donation behavior to Furnas's ideological infrastructure. The paper fits that view: high-opacity C4s look like vehicles for a few donors and route money into PACs. His 2026-07-18 decision to exclude 501c recipients is not stale, since it was a deliberate scope choice. But it predates any reading of this paper. The paper shows that the excluded group contains some highly political conduits, while giving no validated way to identify them. So there is a question to put to Paul (whether to show a display-only split), not a change to make.

related.why: Couch, Fox and Everton model the dark-money network as a graph, and both papers draw on the OpenSecrets/Choma network evidence. That paper supplies the network structure; Irvin supplies an organization-level opacity measure.
Both papers separate an organization's spending channels (lobbying, PAC, nonprofit vehicle). Furnas finds little overlap between lobbying and PAC spending; Irvin adds C4 grants as a third channel.
Both concern the outside-spending regime after Citizens United. Blackwell estimates what the ads do; Irvin measures how hidden the C4 vehicles that fund such spending are.
Crypto industry Super PAC money (Fairshake) is the Mentat setting where C4 and Super PAC routing matters most. Chohan describes the actors; Irvin gives a way to judge how opaque the vehicles are.
Both describe political finance concentrated among a few wealthy donors. Bonica shows this in disclosed giving; Irvin infers it for undisclosed C4 funding.
